item.title: These 7 built-in Windows tools are better than the apps most people install instead
item.itunes:title: These 7 built-in Windows tools are better than the apps most people install instead
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For the longest time, we have been conditioned to believe the built-in Windows tools are somehow inferior to third-party options. That's a major reason behind the popularity of programs like CCleaner for clearing unnecessary files or ShareX for capturing screenshots. Frankly, I have got nothing against these third-party tools. They may work for some — even I use a couple of them — but it's also important to note that native Windows tools have improved significantly over the years.

If you have relied on third-party tools for years because the native options didn't complement your workflow, it's perhaps time to give them another try, especially the ones that have recently received major upgrades. And let me be clear: I am not talking about Microsoft's AI push. There are other genuine improvements as well. Besides, even the old Windows utilities work best in many cases, outperforming most third-party tools.

Disk Cleanup and Storage Sense

For clearing unnecessary files

Let's start with something, I guess, most of us have used at some point: a disk-cleaning software. They do help to a certain extent, but it's not like Windows can't handle that. Ever since the early days of Windows, we have had the Disk Cleanup utility, which can help clear a large amount of unnecessary data and system cache. And its successor, Storage Sense, first introduced in Windows 10 and then carried over to Windows 11, is even better at the job. Storage Sense allows you to automate the process, with Windows automatically deleting unnecessary files at a set frequency.

So, if you are still using a third-party tool to clear storage on your Windows PC, do give it a try. In my experience, the two, or even just Storage Sense, should suffice. As for finding other non-system files that are hogging your PC's storage, a disk analyzer tool like WizTree will help. Try to avoid third-party programs that automatically clear the data for you, as they can sometimes introduce instability.

15 Windows software tools you’ve never heard of but should be using

Discover 15 hidden gem tools for Windows that boost productivity, enhance privacy, and simplify tasks.

17
By  Pranav Bhardwaj

Resource Monitor and Task Manager

For managing resource consumption

If you have been trying to analyze your system's performance or fix random slowdowns, third-party tools may seem like a good option, but Windows already has two tools dedicated to the job: Task Manager and Resource Monitor. The former is a simple, user-friendly utility that shows you the list of active processes, the resources each process is consuming, general system information, and lets you manage startup apps. I am guessing most already know how it works. But many of you may not have used the Resource Monitor.

Resource Monitor is an advanced, built-in tool that provides more detailed insight into the underlying cause rather than giving you a simple overview of the problem. I agree, Resource Monitor's UI may make it feel like the tool is designed for power users, but, frankly, it's not complex. The Overview tab, which loads by default, gives you a general picture, while the dedicated CPU, Memory, Disk, and Network tabs give you detailed insights into what's consuming the resources and the reason behind it.

6 underrated Windows tools you're not using

You owe it to yourself to check these out

2
By  João Carrasqueira

Snipping Tool

For screenshots and recordings

Another Windows utility I have rarely seen people use is Snipping Tool. Natively available on all Windows 10 and 11 PCs, Snipping Tool lets you capture screenshots and record videos of the screen. If that's something you often have to do, Snipping Tool is worth considering over third-party options, and there are several reasons for that.

For the longest time, I solely used ShareX to capture screenshots for articles. It's open-source, easy to use, and offers a bunch of annotation options, while Snipping Tool was, simply put, bare-bones for years. But that's no longer the case. Snipping Tool is now better than ever, with Microsoft adding features like automatic borders, a color picker, a text extractor, annotations, and more. So, the next time you are about to capture a screenshot, use the Windows + Shift + S hotkey and give Snipping Tool a try.

4 reasons I'm still using Snipping Tool instead of the technically better alternatives

There are technically better options out there, but Snipping Tool is perfect for my needs.

2
By  Adam Conway

Notepad

It has improved a lot in recent years

Notepad is something I have always relied on for drafting articles, and I can't even think of ditching the text editor for third-party alternatives, even though decent options exist. The best part about Notepad is its simplicity. Despite Microsoft making a bunch of changes to Notepad in Windows 11, the text editor remains easy to use, which, honestly, can't be said about every native tool.

As for the recent changes, I consider most of these genuine improvements. For instance, with the new formatting options and built-in spellcheck, initial drafts turn out much better. That said, I do feel that Notepad's spellcheck is not perfect, and Microsoft should further refine it.

Notepad's best feature is its simplicity — and I'm worried Microsoft is slowly taking it away

Are we going too far?

2
By  João Carrasqueira

Reliability Monitor and Event Viewer

To identify and troubleshoot issues with the system

Lastly, Windows has two excellent native tools to help you troubleshoot issues with the system: Reliability Monitor and Event Viewer. These don't fix the problem for you, but the utilities help you identify the underlying cause. Between the two, I suggest using Reliability Monitor first.

Reliability Monitor offers a more user-friendly interface and helps you quickly identify what's wrong with the system or the component/app that's failing. Once you have a general idea, use Event Viewer to get into the details and track the problem's history. For the average user, this is the best approach. And in most cases, the two negate the need for third-party tools.

Windows has a built-in troubleshooting tool most people never open

It's more user-friendly than Event Viewer, clearly highlighting critical issues with the system

By  Kazim Alvi

Windows tools can effectively handle most jobs

I don't think people install third-party tools because native Windows utilities aren't as effective or user-friendly. Personally, I believe it has more to do with how third-party tools are promoted. When you see something labeled as a one-click or AI-powered solution, you are bound to favor it over a utility that has looked the same for the last decade. Also, you are missing that, in many cases, the third-party tool essentially relies on core Windows components to do the job. So, why not eliminate the middleman and let Windows take care of the stuff, at least the things it can effectively handle?

item.title: I use these Excel functions and macros to save hours every day
item.itunes:title: I use these Excel functions and macros to save hours every day
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I used to think I was pretty efficient in Excel until I started noticing how much time I wasted on repetitive work. I cleaned up columns, pulled values from different tables, fixed formatting, checked for duplicates, and ran the same little routines over and over again.

Once I started using the right functions and building a few simple macros, that busywork almost disappeared. These are the functions and macros that made the biggest difference to my daily workflow.

6 functions that make Excel feel like magic

These Excel formulas and functions make me feel like a wizard

By  Megan Ellis

XLOOKUP

Saves me from manual searching

XLOOKUP is one of those Excel functions I wish I had started using much earlier. I used to rely on VLOOKUP for most of my lookup tasks, but it comes with unnecessary limitations. The lookup column needs to sit in a specific position; I have to think about column numbers, and inserting a new column can sometimes break the formula.

XLOOKUP feels far more flexible. I simply tell Excel what value I am looking for, where to find it, and which corresponding value I want returned. It can look left or right, uses exact matches by default, and lets me define what should appear when Excel can’t find a match.

That becomes a serious time-saver when I am dealing with large spreadsheets. For example, suppose I have a master sheet with hundreds of products, including product IDs, prices, suppliers, and stock levels.

On another sheet, I might only have a list of product IDs for an upcoming order. Instead of jumping between sheets and manually searching for every product, I can use XLOOKUP to automatically pull the latest price and supplier details into my order sheet.

If I add 50 more products, I don’t need to repeat the process manually. I just extend the formula, and Excel does the searching for me.

If the product ID I want to look up is in cell A2, I can pull its price from the master sheet with the formula below.

=XLOOKUP(A2, Master!A:A,Master!B:B, “Not found”)

UNIQUE

Cleans up the list instantly

UNIQUE is another Excel function that saves me from doing repetitive cleanup every time I work with a large list. It does exactly what its name suggests. It scans a range, returns only distinct values, and creates a clean list automatically.

More importantly, the result is dynamic. If I add new entries to the original data, Excel can update the UNIQUE output without me running Remove Duplicates again.

Suppose I have a sales sheet where Column B contains customer names. Because the same customers may have placed multiple orders, their names can appear dozens of times. If I want a clean customer list for another report, I can simply use =UNIQUE(B2:B1000) and Excel immediately gives me one instance of every customer in that range.

I can make it even more useful by combining it with SORT.

=SORT(UNIQUE(B2:B1000)) and now Excel arranges them alphabetically without touching the original data.

FILTER

Builds reports without manual sorting

FILTER is one of my favorite Excel functions when I need to pull a specific set of records from a much larger table. I used to rely heavily on Excel’s regular filter controls. This function removes most of the manual work because I can create a separate, dynamic view of the exact records I need.

For instance, suppose I have a sales sheet where column A contains order IDs, column B has customer names, column C contains order values, and column D shows the payment status. If I want to create a separate list containing only unpaid orders, I can use:

=FILTER(A2:D1000,D2:D1000= "Unpaid", "No unpaid orders")

Excel quickly pulls every row where the status is marked as Unpaid. I can also make the formula more specific. I can even add a condition and make it display unpaid orders worth more than $1000.

Data-cleanup macro

Fix messy spreadsheets automatically

A data-cleanup macro is probably one of the biggest time-savers in my Excel workflow because messy spreadsheets are almost unavoidable. I regularly end up with files that have extra spaces, duplicate rows, inconsistent formatting, blank records, text stored as numbers, or columns that are too narrow to read properly.

This is where I use a simple cleanup macro. I can record one that removes blank rows, trims unnecessary spaces, deletes duplicates, converts values into the correct format, applies consistent number formatting, and auto-fits the columns in one go.

Instead of working through the spreadsheet manually, I run the macro once and let Excel handle the housekeeping for me.

9 Excel hacks I wish I knew earlier

Excel tricks to save you hours every week

3
By  Parth Shah

Report-preparation macro

Automate an entire workflow

A report-preparation macro is where Excel automation starts to feel powerful for me. Instead of using a macro for one small action, I can bundle an entire reporting routine into a single command.

For example, I might have a monthly sales report that pulls refreshed data, sorts transactions by date, highlights high-value orders, adjusts column widths, updates the report date, refreshes PivotTables, and finally exports the finished sheet as a PDF.

Without automation, that workflow can involve dozens of clicks and plenty of room for mistakes.

Excel now handles the boring stuff

Excel becomes far more useful once I stop treating every task as something I need to do manually. Functions like XLOOKUP, UNIQUE, and FILTER already remove a lot of repetitive work, while macros take it further by automating entire cleanup and reporting routines.

item.itunes:title: I stopped hiding movies from friends and started giving them their own Jellyfin view instead
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My media library is a highly curated experience set up to meet my precise needs. I download, organize, and add movies and TV shows to the library, and Jellyfin handles playback across devices. Over time, I've given close friends and family members access to this library, which has, unfortunately, created its own set of problems.

For one, I don't want everyone who has access to my Jellyfin library to see everything I have. I'm a big fan of horror cinema, but some of the gore-rich content can be a bit much for some of my friends. Meanwhile, creating individual libraries is certainly possible, but it's way too cumbersome for me to be bothered with it.

Clearly, there had to be a better way to handle this. That's where JellyPrivateLibraries steps in. The app gives each Jellyfin user a private selection of media from my existing library without needing to create separate libraries. It's an astonishingly clean solution to a very common problem.

Set up JellyPrivateLibraries in minutes

Give every user their own view of Jellyfin

Credit: 

Installing JellyPrivateLibraries is straightforward using Jellyfin's built-in plugin system. Just add the repository from the GitHub link, tap add, and you're done. From there, if you want, you can connect your JellySeerr instance for more granular control, but we'll get to that in a minute. Let's take a step back and discuss the why of it.

Giving access to my media library has traditionally meant giving access to everything. That doesn't make sense all the time. If someone just wants an easy way to watch a few classic comedies, having them sift through a hundred thrillers is pointless.

Credit: 

With JellyPrivateLibraries, I can create a restricted experience for individual users. Instead of creating a segregated physical library, the plugin uses Jellyfin's existing per-user tag permissions, so each restricted user gets a personal tag. The plugin then assigns that tag to individual movies, allowing Jellyfin to filter movies by user. That might sound complex on paper, but the setup is surprisingly simple.

Once I enable the private library for a user, JellyPrivateLibraries adds a widget to Jellyfin that lets users manage their own content selection. There's no need to create a new library or move files around. This widget can handle all the filtering in place. Predictably, this works both ways. While a user can certainly filter out the content they don't want to see, I can also hide content from non-admin users using Jellyfin's blocked tag functionality, making it a much more sensible way of sharing a large media library.

I stopped choosing between Plex and Jellyfin, and my media server is better because of it

Both Plex and Jellyfin are better when you stop trying to choose between them

Manual controls are certainly handy, but the system really comes into its own when you combine it with Seerr. While Seerr isn't required for the plugin to work, it elevates the experience by combining requests, media libraries, and individual preferences into a single setup. Moreover, since I've already automated my friends' incessant movie requests, adding Seerr to the mix makes a lot of sense for me, and I suspect it does for most other users.

If you're unfamiliar with Seerr, the service gives users a dedicated interface for browsing movies and TV shows and requesting that content in Jellyfin. The service connects to the likes of Radarr and Sonarr for the actual processing, but that's out of the scope of this article. What's more relevant is JellyPrivateLibraries' integration with Seerr. Once you've set up the relevant API tokens, a friend can open Seerr and request a movie. Once it is downloaded, JellyPrivateLibraries then automatically assigns that movie to the user who requested it. The plugin supports Seerr webhooks for this purpose and can even sync back previous requests.

Credit: 

This is where the setup starts making a lot of sense. I don't have to keep tabs on who requested what and if I want it crowding up the main library. Nor do I have to wait for a movie to download and then manually find it in Jellyfin. The entire process, including the request, gets automated and saves me time and effort.

Let's assume a friend has a taste for unique art house cinema. In a normal scenario, those same movies would fill up the homepage for all users once added to my library. Now, using a combination of JellyPrivateLibraries and Seerr, they can build an entire collection on my server that's visible only to them. It's great for taming a large library.

Building the perfect shared media server

My Jellyfin setup is central to my self-hosted stack, and for a long time, I thought I was done tinkering with it. The media downloads and playback were fully automated, and my content was fully organized. But the problem of clutter and lack of curated libraries was something that bothered me.

Credit: 

JellyPrivateLibraries solves that without needing me to change anything else in my setup. It seamlessly integrates into my existing library and organization. I can keep one large media library, give individual users their own selection, and let Jellyfin handle the rest. I can configure it to share my entire library, none of it, or somewhere in between, and it takes me no more than a few minutes to do it. Can't beat that.

item.title: Obsidian's best features have nothing to do with note-taking, and they replaced my entire workflow
item.itunes:title: Obsidian's best features have nothing to do with note-taking, and they replaced my entire workflow
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Nearly every guide for Obsidian out there assumes you're there to take notes, which is fair enough, it is a markdown editor after all. But once you've been in the app for a while, you realize the note-taking becomes the least interesting thing about it, and dare I even say the least useful thing about it. Given that the vault is just a regular folder with plain text files, JSON files, and perhaps a couple of image files on your disk, you have complete freedom to create any setup you want and because Obsidian just reads the folder, whatever setup you build shows up inside the app itself too, creating the perfect workflow loop…

4 game-changing Obsidian workflows I wish I tried earlier

Obsidian workflows I tried late, but you don’t have to

4
By  Parth Shah

The vault as a project manager

I don't need an elaborate productivity stack anymore

I used to jump between Obsidian for notes and something else for actually tracking what I was working on, usually Notion and Trello. But each additional tool was another thing to manage, if I even remembered to open it every morning.

Then I realized the vault already had every piece of information those apps needed, it was just scattered across folders with no view on top of it. So I made a folder called /index/ and used it as a dashboard layer, with a separate markdown file for active projects, stalled work, this week's priorities, orphaned notes, and a couple more. Every dashboard is just markdown with a table and wikilinks, which means it renders natively in Obsidian without needing Dataview or Bases or any plugin (though the Bases plugin plays really well with this setup should you need a more detailed view).

The reason this isn't a maintenance chore for me like project tracking was in other apps is that I use Claude Code to build and maintain the dashboards for me. It crawls my vault, checks the frontmatter and modification times, and updates the tables whenever something's changed. So, for example, if I add a deadline to a design project brief in Obsidian and ask Claude to regenerate, my "this-week.md" picks it up instantly.

Another very welcome side effect of this setup that I didn't see coming is that /index/ became the visual center of my vault in the graph view. I never bothered much with the graph view because mine always used to be a disconnected and scattered mess, but this actually gives me something cohesive that I can properly navigate, plus it just looks really cool.

I found these 5 incredible open source Obsidian alternatives so that you don’t have to

Finding Obsidian’s open source twin

5
By  Parth Shah

The vault as a cache

Probably the most useful thing I added to my vault

Most of the Obsidian-plus-AI pieces you'll read are about feeding your notes into a chatbot, which is fine, I've written a few of those myself. But the setup I actually use runs in the opposite direction. My vault stores answers that Claude Code has already produced so it doesn't have to redo the work.

The mechanism is dead simple. There's a /Cache/ folder, and there's a CLAUDE.md file at the vault root that tells Claude Code to save synthesis-heavy answers as named markdown notes, and to check that folder first before re-reading raw sources.

Practically, that means fewer rate limits, which is why I set it up in the first place. So now I'm not burning tokens making Claude re-read the same 20 or 30 files every time I ask a version of the same question. That alone made it worth doing, but there's another part to this that makes it more useful…

What I find more interesting is what those cache notes actually are once they exist. They're regular markdown files in a folder in my vault, which means I can treat them the way I treat any other note, and they get backed up by the same syncing tools (Google Drive and Syncthing for me, depending on which vault I'm working with). So if any of my AI agents or tools went down tomorrow, the folder will still be there and backed up, with all the knowledge I've gained from my sessions. So it's cached work that's now mine, instead of a chat history stuck in a provider's app.

How I set up a local wiki for my projects using Obsidian

My secret weapon for project mastery

By  Parth Shah

Sketching UX flows, wireframes, and diagrams

Canvas isn't just a whiteboard

I've been using Obsidian Canvas for low-fi wireframes and UX flow diagrams lately, mostly because opening Figma for a rough sketch feels a little overboard. Canvas gives me what I want at the early-thinking stage without the layout gymnastics that comes from a proper design tool. It's a super clean and easy space to navigate with minimal tooling, so I can throw around color-coded cards and connect them in minutes.

What pushed this from a nice-to-have into something I actually build with is that .canvas files are just JSON. Obsidian published the spec as JSON Canvas back in March 2024. It's genuinely simple, two top-level arrays (one for nodes, one for edges), a handful of node types like text and file and group, and coordinates in pixels.

Once again, I'm circling back to Claude here, because you can open .canvas files directly in Claude Code. In fact, I copy them over to my design directories where I've already had beefy sessions on the design brief, perhaps a bit of vibe-coding experimentation, and then Claude can help me write the JSON for user flows, personas, and low-fi wireframes. Then I simply copy the .canvas file back into my vault, and voila, now I have a foundation that I can tweak however I see fit inside the Obsidian app with the Canvas plugin.

Months into Obsidian, I finally discovered features I should've used from day one

Powerful features were hiding in plain sight

By  Patrick Hearn

The most-used features in my vault have nothing to do with note-taking

Every one of these use cases exists because I could point another tool at the same folder and have it do something useful with what's already there. It's the same reason people still write plain text a decade after Markdown stopped being novel; the openness compounds.

item.title: 60GHz radar finally solved the problem that's been killing smart home lighting for years
item.itunes:title: 60GHz radar finally solved the problem that's been killing smart home lighting for years
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you use motion sensors for the lights in your home, you've probably experienced being plunged into total darkness because your motion sensor assumes the room is empty when you're sitting still or resting. Traditional passive infrared sensors aren't presence sensors; they are motion detectors, meaning they look for shifting infrared heat signatures. If you aren't actively moving, you become invisible.

Early mm wave sensors seemed like the solution, but they lacked spatial awareness. They could tell someone was in the room but not where. Now high-frequency 60GHz mmWave sensors broadcast tiny-wavelength radio packets and can analyze complex phase shifts. They don't just detect presence; they map a room into custom coordinate grids, track sub-millimeter chest movements from breathing, and pinpoint coordinates in real time without the need to DIY.

Basic motion sensors treat a room as a binary on/off box. High-frequency 60GHz mmWave radars act as a localized spatial grid, shifting home automation from simple motion triggers to true room awareness, multi-zone tracking, and micro-motion intelligence.

I built an ESP32-powered presence sensor using only Bluetooth, here's how it works

I can now detect when I enter a room, using just an ESP32 and ESPHome.

6
By  Adam Conway

PIR sensors feel outdated

mmWave is the way forward

Traditional motion sensors typically use passive infrared, often referred to as PIR. They rely on pyroelectric elements to detect differential changes in ambient infrared radiation, but this comes with a flaw. It means that the sensors are blind to static objects and require gross physical displacement across segments to trip. If you're sitting still for a while, the sensor will fail to recognize that you're even in the room at all.

Originally, a 24GHz mmWave sensor felt like a revolutionary step, and it was simple to DIY if you wanted. It uses longer radio wavelengths that excel at general macro presence detection through drywall and light obstructions, but it was still a compromise because it lacks the high spatial resolution needed for precise multi-zone tracking or subtle gesture recognition.

Now with 60GHz high-resolution phased arrays, they operate at extremely short millimeter wavelengths using printed patch antenna arrays that form concentrated directional beams. This brings an exceptional level of automation because it lets the radar capture micro-Doppler shifts, distinguishing between a walking human, a swaying houseplant, and the gentle expansion of a human chest cavity during breathing.

What can you actually do with mmWave?

It gives you access to so many features

It's all well and good having access to this technology, but what can you actually do with it in your smart home? It provides you with advanced capabilities that really separate 60 GHz sensors from standard automation hardware.

The first is multi-zone room mapping, which lets you activate virtual tripwires. Advanced 60GHz units allow users to slice a single room into up to 30 distinct detection zones via companion apps or Home Assistant. In real-world use, Zone A (like the sofa) turns on ambient reading lights at 20%. Zone B (like the desk) turns on task lighting at 100%, and Zone C (like the doorway) triggers entry paths. You don't need separate sensors for different areas of the room anymore.

You also have multi-target tracking because you can track up to five separate individuals simultaneously within the same spatial matrix, updating coordinates as people move across different furniture layout quadrants. Of course, these sensors also track your vitals and provide fall detection. That way, it can measure respiration rate, specifically breaths per minute, as well as micro-displacements to enable fall detection or sleep monitoring without invasive video cameras in your bedroom.

It's not all perfect

There are points of friction when setting up a 60GHz mmWave sensor

A 60GHz mmWave sensor might sound like it's from the future, but real-world friction points come up when you deploy a high-frequency radar like this. Sometimes you can experience false positives because 60GHz radars are sensitive enough to detect micro movements. An oscillating desk fan, blowing window curtains, or even pets moving across a room can trigger false occupancy states. If sensitivity filters aren't tuned properly, it may take some getting used to when you first install your sensor, as you'll need to adjust the filters to what works for your home.

Also, unlike omnidirectional PIR bulbs, the 60GHz phased arrays have specific beam patterns. Proper mounting height, tilt angle, and exclusion zones are critical to prevent radar reflection off of hard tile floors and glass windows. These surfaces can skew coordinate maps and make the mapping you set up essentially unusable.

Despite the fact that you get access to a whole new range of features, the setup process for these sensors can be a little bit more finicky and frustrating. But once you have them ready to go, they are fantastic.

No more waving your arms around in darkness

A new sensor will give you access to so many more automations

For decades, smart home automation has been hamstrung by seemingly binary motion switches, but upgrading to 60GHz mmWave radar can change the paradigm entirely. One sensor can introduce multiple automation settings for an entire room as it becomes a spatially aware environment that reacts to human presence with surgical precision. If you're still using legacy PIR motion detectors in your primary living spaces, then you might benefit from installing a 60GHz radar sensor, mapping your room's active zones, and experiencing a smart home that actually knows that you're in the room even when you're sitting still.

item.title: Your PSU still follows a color-coding standard that’s decades older than your PC, but there's a reason why
item.itunes:title: Your PSU still follows a color-coding standard that’s decades older than your PC, but there's a reason why
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The importance of using a quality power supply is obvious to even new PC builders. It's the component that protects your expensive hardware from potentially devastating electrical shenanigans. What's way less obvious is the underlying make-up of the wires running from the PSU to the motherboard. These wires follow a standard established before some of you were even born.

The color codes of power supply wires haven't changed in over three decades because, well, there's no reason to do it. These colors are crucial for technicians and tinkerers, simplifying troubleshooting and repurposing projects. The standard doesn't need to evolve; it is doing exactly what it needs to do by staying constant.

Got a new PSU? Reusing your old cables is a gamble you shouldn't take

Mixing PSU cables between different models can be fatal

1
By  Tanveer Singh

ATX traces its roots back to the AT standard from the 80s

We're using 30-year-old color codes

Credit: Wikimedia Commons

The "modern" ATX (Advanced Technology Standard) standard was introduced by Intel in 1995 to improve on the older AT (Advanced Technology) standard by IBM in 1984. The latter forced PC builders to be extremely careful when plugging the PSU connectors to the motherboard. If you plugged them backwards, you would instantly fry the motherboard.

Besides, the stiff PSU cables connected to a heavy power toggle switch on the PC case, and could cause a short circuit if miswired. The ATX standard retained the black, red, yellow, and blue wires from the AT standard while introducing orange, purple, green, and gray wires for modern hardware.

Common wires in AT and ATX

New wires added in ATX

Black (ground)

Orange (+3.3V DC)

Red (+5V DC)

Purple (+5V standby)

Yellow (+12V DC)

Green (Power Supply On)

Blue (-12V DC)

Gray (Power Good)

Modern CPUs and RAM didn't need as much voltage, so the new 3.3V voltage rail was added in the ATX standard. The purple wire brought standby power to PSUs, which was missing in the older standard. The green wire allowed the motherboard to turn the PSU on or off via software. And the gray wire signaled the motherboard that all voltages were stable and it was safe for the processor to boot up.

In fact, the even more ancient Molex connectors used the same basic color-coding: yellow for +12V, red for +5V, and black for ground. The ATX standard didn't invent a completely new standard; it built on decades of convention.

The 6 worst PC hardware trends that rightfully disappeared

Some of the worst PC hardware trends had their time in the sun, and then got their deserving place in PC history

8
By  Tanveer Singh

You don't need to identify PSU wires by color, except when you do

If you're the tinkering type

Credit: Wikimedia Commons

To be fair, most people will never have to refer to the internal color-coding of their PSU cables. It's not something that comes up in regular PC use, or even when you're building a PC. PSUs have evolved from shipping with stiff, non-modular cables to flexible modular ones. PC builders don't know what's going on inside the cables, but some people make use of this decades-old standard whenever they're doing something out of the ordinary.

Suppose you're repurposing an old PSU as a bench power supply or diagnosing a dead PC with a multimeter. You'd want to know which wire is going where when the connector shape doesn't tell you everything. The ancient color code helps you identify what you're touching before you touch it.

My PSU just blew up - here's what I'll do to avoid that happening again

My PSU blew up after less than five years, and it changed how I'll approach PSUs forever.

13
By  Andre Revilla

It's a relic of the PC industry, but it has practical uses

If it ain't broke, don't fix it

PSU color-coding isn't random — it's designed as a safety and troubleshooting system. The colors haven't changed in over three decades because PCs still use the same voltages they did back then. The underlying electronic architecture hasn't changed, so there is no physical reason to invent a new color code.

Moreover, the industry inertia keeps things constant. New color codes will mean retraining technicians, changing component manuals, and educating users to avoid errors when sleeving cables. It will be a massive exercise with no practical benefit. So, keeping things unchanged isn't just a safety mechanism; it also avoids needless expense.

While this color-coding convention is near-universally followed, it's not strictly enforced. For instance, some Dell PCs use PSUs with non-standard color assignments on ATX connectors. This can make swapping Dell PSUs with a standard ATX unit highly risky. By and large, though, the three-decade-old standard has kept PSU wiring standardized, safe, and simple.

The weakest link in your PC might not be what you think

Cheap or outdated cables might be ruining your PC's safety and performance

By  Tanveer Singh

The ATX standard is more than just a convention

For over thirty years, the same color-coding standard has been at play inside almost every single PSU. The ATX standard introduced a new voltage rail and several new wires to account for newer hardware iterations. It has helped countless technicians and troubleshooters play with their hardware safely and responsibly.

The green wire allowed the motherboard to turn the PSU on or off via software. And the gray wire signaled the motherboard that all voltages were stable and it was safe for the processor to boot up.

In fact, the even more ancient Molex connectors used the same basic color-coding: yellow for +12V, red for +5V, and black for ground. The ATX standard didn't invent a completely new standard; it built on decades of convention.

The 6 worst PC hardware trends that rightfully disappeared

Some of the worst PC hardware trends had their time in the sun, and then got their deserving place in PC history

8
By  Tanveer Singh

You don't need to identify PSU wires by color, except when you do

If you're the tinkering type

Credit: Wikimedia Commons

To be fair, most people will never have to refer to the internal color-coding of their PSU cables. It's not something that comes up in regular PC use, or even when you're building a PC. PSUs have evolved from shipping with stiff, non-modular cables to flexible modular ones. PC builders don't know what's going on inside the cables, but some people make use of this decades-old standard whenever they're doing something out of the ordinary.

Suppose you're repurposing an old PSU as a bench power supply or diagnosing a dead PC with a multimeter. You'd want to know which wire is going where when the connector shape doesn't tell you everything. The ancient color code helps you identify what you're touching before you touch it.

My PSU blew up after less than five years, and it changed how I'll approach PSUs forever.

It's a relic of the PC industry, but it has practical uses

If it ain't broke, don't fix it

PSU color-coding isn't random — it's designed as a safety and troubleshooting system. The colors haven't changed in over three decades because PCs still use the same voltages they did back then. The underlying electronic architecture hasn't changed, so there is no physical reason to invent a new color code.

Moreover, the industry inertia keeps things constant. New color codes will mean retraining technicians, changing component manuals, and educating users to avoid errors when sleeving cables. It will be a massive exercise with no practical benefit. So, keeping things unchanged isn't just a safety mechanism; it also avoids needless expense.

While this color-coding convention is near-universally followed, it's not strictly enforced. For instance, some Dell PCs use PSUs with non-standard color assignments on ATX connectors. The weakest link in your PC might not be what you think

Cheap or outdated cables might be ruining your PC's safety and performance

By  Tanveer Singh

The ATX standard is more than just a convention

For over thirty years, the same color-coding standard has been at play inside almost every single PSU. The ATX standard introduced a new voltage rail and several new wires to account for newer hardware iterations. It has helped countless technicians and troubleshooters play with their hardware safely and responsibly.

item.itunes:title: Qualcomm split its 2026 flagship Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chip into two tiers, with the Extreme version packing 50% more shared memory
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Qualcomm's 2026 high-end mobile lineup includes two top chips: the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and the Elite Extreme Gen 6.
  • The Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 targets top phones with agentic AI: new Hexagon NPU, 30B+ MoE parameters, and 50% larger shared memory.
  • Both chips top out at 5.0GHz for their prime cores and 4.0GHz for their performance cores.

Qualcomm is shaking up its flagship mobile lineup in 2026 with two top-tier mobile chips: the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6.

According to the chipmaker, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 targets the highest-end smartphones on the market. While the company hasn't named specific devices beyond the China-exclusive Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max (which aren't coming to the U.S.), and Motorola's Signature 27 (it's making its way to the U.S.), we'll likely see the new chip in ultra-high-end smartphones like Samsung's inevitable but still-unannounced Galaxy S27 Ultra.

Meanwhile, the less powerful but still flagship Elite Gen 6 chip is positioned as this year's standard top-tier offering, and will probably land in pretty much every high-end smartphone released in 2027 that isn't an iPhone or a Pixel.

Qualcomm says the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 delivers substantial gains in performance and graphics efficiency, with an emphasis on the "new era of agentic AI." Additionally, the chipmaker claims the powerful chip's NPU can run Mixture-of-Experts models with more than 30 billion parameters and features 50% larger shared memory.

Qualcomm says the future of smartphones is proactive AI intent, not apps

The chipmaker placed a big emphasis on its continued relationship with Google

Credit: Qualcomm

During the Snapdragon Summit 2026 keynote mobile presentation, Cristiano Amon, Qualcomm's CEO and President of Qualcomm Incorporated, outlined how the company sees the future of smartphones as focused on proactive AI intent, rather than apps, and said its new chips are designed with these next-generation agentic experiences in mind.

The company also emphasized its partnership with Google, bringing Rick Osterloh onstage to reinforce Qualcomm and the Mountain View-based company's continued partnership. That said, the conversation between Amon and Osterloh offered no new revelations beyond hyping up Gemini and the concept of Agentic AI.

"It's less about navigating apps and more about completing tasks for you, and it's going to handle a lot of the details required to get things done for you," said Amon during the opening section of the keynote. "Whether the agent runs on the device or is built into the OS, it needs to do a lot of coordination, but your experiences need to remain useful, instantly secure, and always available."

On the gaming side, Qualcomm outlined that the Extreme Gen 6 adds AI-dedicated Adreno matrix cores that power features like AI super resolution and frame generation through Adreno Neural Fusion. The chipmaker mentions a few specific mobile games that support these features, including Diablo Immortal, War Thunder Mobile, and Farming Simulator 26. Peak speeds with the Oryon CPU top out at 5.0GHz for the prime cores and 4.0GHz for the performance cores.

From a camera perspective, the new chip is the first to let a smartphone camera capture 8K/60fps. The Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 also supports cinema-grade video with APV and 4K/240fps slow-motion video.

The base Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 also features notable upgrades

Like its higher-end counterpart, the 8 Elite Gen 6 is all about agentic AI

While the Snapdragon Elite Extreme Gen 6 is this year's top-tier chip, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 also includes several notable new features. Like its more powerful counterpart, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 is designed to understand personal context across devices and emphasizes tailored agentic AI that learns and adapts to you over time.

Other key features include zero-prompt AI photo editing and a new agentic AI-focused Hexagon Element Accelerator. Like the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, the Elite Gen 6 also features the X105 5G Modem-RF, which Qualcomm says paves the way for next-gen 6G AI-enhanced connectivity. However, it's still unclear how AI fits into the next-generation wireless standard.

The first Googlebook laptops are coming from Acer, Asus Dell, and HP.

item.title: Most Raspberry Pi projects will never touch the extra RAM you're paying for
item.itunes:title: Most Raspberry Pi projects will never touch the extra RAM you're paying for
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When I bought the 8GB variant of the Raspberry Pi 5 at launch, I got it pretty close to its official price tag, and it’s the one I use the most to benchmark random distros and unsupported emulators. Unfortunately, if I were to buy the same single-board computer today, I’d probably have to pay close to $200 (and even more, once you toss the active cooler and storage accessories into the equation),

However, I’ve been experimenting with cheaper Raspberry Pi models for a while, and models with lower RAM are nowhere near as terrible as you’d think. Sure, running the likes of Windows 11 ARM on a 1GB Raspberry Pi is bound to result in performance issues. But the majority of Raspberry Pi projects you’d find online don’t siphon anywhere close to the memory on high-end models.

I tried using my Raspberry Pi as a laptop

With the right hardware and OS, even a Raspberry Pi can serve as solid daily driver

13
By  Ayush Pande

Projects involving sensors and DMA peripherals don’t need a lot of RAM

You don’t need an expensive RPi model for your display and camera accessories

If you’re fascinated with the GPIO pins, DSI/CSI (or depending on your board, MIPI) connectors, and other cool interfaces on your Raspberry Pi, most of the projects utilizing them work well on low-end boards that aren’t blessed in the memory department. Let’s say you’re trying to build a setup that displays a dashboard on a screen plugged into a DSI slot on your Raspberry Pi. Unless you’re attempting to run a bulky website with hundreds of pages that each save new records to a database, you shouldn’t have a lot of trouble hosting a tiny Flask/LAMP web server on a RAM-deficient board and sending the output to a tiny DSI-compatible screen.

Likewise, for folks trying to build a timelapse camera, you can pair any ol’ module capable of snapping pictures with the CSI interface. Then, you can write a small script that captures a new image every few seconds, and voilà, even a cheap RPi can get the job done.

Of course, the situation is vastly different if you’re trying to run Frigate or other NVR tools to manage live video feeds from the camera or an AI accelerator to analyze the recordings. But leaving these scenarios aside, most display and camera projects are so simple that you can even use the humble Raspberry Pi Zero and get solid results, even though the Zero lineup has painfully low RAM.

Then you’ve got sensor-heavy projects, which follow the same principle. For example, when I built a weather station using my Raspberry Pi 5 and a BME280 sensor a few years ago, I could’ve substituted an RPi Zero (one with soldered GPIO pins), and the result would’ve been the same regardless of the board. In fact, a large part of the RAM allocation would go to the underlying Linux distribution, while the sensors and their code barely need any memory.

4 Raspberry Pi projects I abandoned after realizing sub-$150 mini PCs run them all better

After all, cheap mini-PCs crush Raspberry Pi SBCs on the performance and OS compatibility fronts

28
By  Ayush Pande

Lightweight services run just fine on low-end Raspberry Pi units

Especially when you opt for an ultra-lightweight distribution

When I first got into self-hosting free and open-source apps as Docker containers, I figured I’d need a lot of RAM on the host machine. That’s not necessarily incorrect, because certain bulky services can hog memory like there’s no tomorrow. But there are just as many lightweight tools you can deploy on RAM-constrained boards.

Apps such as BentoPDF, IT-Tools, and ConvertX are a godsend for productivity tasks, but you don’t have to spend hundreds of megabytes to deploy them, let alone a gigabyte or two. A complex AdGuard/Pi-hole setup that sees a massive volume of queries from dozens of devices and needs a ginormous collection of block lists might be too much even for a 4GB Raspberry Pi. But for a simple ad-blocker instance that serves a few client devices in a beginner-friendly home lab, you don’t necessarily need a high-end RPi unit laden with RAM.

The same goes for lightweight monitoring services, and the Uptime Kuma + Gotify combo works surprisingly well on most Raspberry Pi boards. If you’re as fond of Proxmox high-availability setups as I am, but only possess two PCs for the cluster, arming any ol’ Raspberry Pi with QDevice packages and letting it serve as a tie-breaker node can let you build a reliable dual-system cluster without worrying about split-brain issues.

Interestingly enough, I recently tried turning the original Raspberry Pi Zero board into a Docker-hosting workstation, and despite adding a few services, the SBC chugged along nicely. If anything, the aged CPU inside the OG RPi Zero model was more of a bottleneck than the 512MB RAM. But when it comes to running a Tailscale subnet router, this cheap SBC is more than enough to cover my entire home lab.

That said, a few Raspberry Pi projects can be absolute RAM hogs

Honestly, most of the projects I’ve covered over the years on XDA would work just as well on a 2-4GB RAM Raspberry Pi unit. That said, certain wacky experiments did require a lot more memory investment. Attempting to run dozens of bulky containers, for example, would crash a low-memory model, and the same applies to DIY Windows 11, TrueNAS, and Proxmox installations. Likewise, I wouldn’t recommend emulating newer 3D consoles on a RAM-constrained Pi or using such a board to run an OpenMediaVault instance loaded with tons of plugins.

Raspberry Pi Zero W
$15 at Micro Center

item.title: 4 lessons I learned the hard way after ditching Plex for Jellyfin
item.itunes:title: 4 lessons I learned the hard way after ditching Plex for Jellyfin
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When it comes to self-hosted media, it's nice to have a choice of server platforms. Plex was the first on the scene in the early days, but Kodi, Emby, and Jellyfin gave us more options. Since Plex paywalled so many features and open-source alternatives are worth a look, I jumped at the ability to ditch Plex and move to the free Jellyfin platform.

However, I wasn't ready for some of the differences there are between self-hosted media platforms. For instance, the Jellyfin server can be more difficult to maintain, and the media population didn't work as easily as I expected. Inevitably, I'm glad I made the switch, since it felt liberating, but more management is involved. If you are on the fence, there are some things you'll want to know first.

Library setup

The structure is more than clicking a few buttons

If you are used to having a messy media library and leaning on Plex to just "figure it out," you're in for a rude awakening with Jellyfin library management. One thing I like about Plex is that I can throw my media into folders, and it figures out what the files are and displays them properly, often without labeling them correctly.

Jellyfin is far less forgiving than Plex when it comes to library setup. For my media library in Jellyfin to truly display properly on its web version and other clients, it needs a proper folder structure, file names, permissions, release dates, metadata, library types, and more. Some movies and TV shows require a metadata-provider ID to prevent the server from misidentifying them.

A folder containing a mix of movies, TV shows, and music videos will usually work with Plex, but with Jellyfin, you need to be more meticulous and keep a clean folder structure. One thing I liked about Plex was ripping a movie into a certain folder and having it show up. I didn't have to rename it. I thought I could do the same with Jellyfin. The first time I brought my media library over from Plex to Jellyfin, a lot of content was misidentified, and some didn't show up at all because of an incorrect naming convention.

Jellyfin
iOS compatible
Yes
Android compatible
Yes
See at Jellyfin Jellyfin 12 (RC5)

Manual Metadata

Some files are stubborn and need manual correction

The good (and bad) thing about Jellyfin is it searches sources like IMDB, OMDB, and TMDB for the content's metadata. It also searches sources like fanart.TV, NFO files, and AniDB.tv for all kinds of art, posters, backdrops, actor information, etc., which adds to the viewing experience. If my movie or show is labeled correctly and in the right folder structure, it's a great feature.

However, this also means you could spend a lot of time manually configuring your media files. There have been many times when I have had to resolve problems with mismatches, missing season titles, wrong episode orders, poor artwork, and more. Helpful tools like TinyMediaManager can get metadata in order, but some files can be particularly stubborn.

One time, I added episodes of House MD to my TV Shows folder, and it misidentified an entire season as a Japanese children's sitcom with incorrect artwork to boot. I could play the shows, but I had to manually delete the wrong metadata and enter the correct IMDb and TVDB provider choices. It's actually happened a couple of times, and I fixed it by adding the IMDb info to the folder name.

TinyMediaManager
See at TinyMediaManager

Jellyfin clients aren't created equal

Some don't display your content at all or work on a device

Since Jellyfin is free and open-source, it has a ton of different clients available. However, they aren't created equal, and some only display certain media on certain devices; they aren't available on all devices, and some don't display your library well. Coming from Plex, I was used to official clients that worked on virtually every device and let me watch my content. The Jellyfin client world is completely different, which is good in some ways and not so much in others.

You will find a Jellyfin client for all mainstream devices, though the experience isn't uniform. On many devices, you can use the official Jellyfin client, which usually works the best. However, it doesn't work the best on every device, so it's good that Jellyfin users have a choice. However, some Jellyfin clients rely on web versions, and third-party alternatives can be hit-or-miss. The one I like best, and that's available on most platforms, is Moonfin, since it also has some cool theming capabilities. While Jellyfin clients are everywhere, it doesn't mean they are equally finished everywhere.

Moonfin
OS
Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS, Android TV, webOS, Tizen
See at Moonfin See at Apple App Store

Remote viewing is free but still at a cost

It's your job to ensure the remote server is securely accessible

Plex put remote viewing of your server's content behind a paywall. To view content from your own server, you need Plex Pass, or anyone you want to watch your content needs a Remote Watch Pass. With Jellyfin, it's all free, which is why I was happy to make the jump. However, you need to spend time and effort making your server secure and available outside the home, which falls on the owner.

To do that, you need a stable LAN, secure port forwarding — via a reverse proxy, VPN, Tailscale (if you dare), or another secure access method. You also have to renew HTTPS certificates, manage server addresses and DNS, test constantly, handle accounts, and more. It can become a lot of work, and you might think a Plex subscription is worth it to avoid the headache. In the end, it comes down to how important remote watching is, how much time you have, and whether it's worth the time and effort for the people using it.

Tailscale
See at Tailscale

Switching from Plex to Jellyfin isn't seamless

There's no doubt that Plex is easier to use for a self-hosted media configuration. You can be sloppy with your media folders with little to no negative effect on your media-viewing enjoyment. Jellyfin requires more work, especially for remote viewing.

But setting up clean libraries and correct metadata can also be involved. However, once you get it, you're happy you did it yourself. But if you don't have the time, patience, or knowledge to run your own server, you might want to skip Jellyfin and just pay for the features.
